title: Assessment of seven minimally sampling protocols of archaeological skeletal proteomes
projectDescription: Archaeological bone material is increasingly being sampled for various molecular analyses. Minimally invasive sampling protocols should therefore be utilised whenever possible. We compare the proteomic output of 10 Early Neolithic Bos sp. humeri, from two different preservation contexts, of seven sampling protocols, namely retrieving bone chips (with and without demineralisation), acid etching (FASP and chemical neutralisation), eraser, membrane box, and polishing film. We note that minimally invasive sampling methods can extract a substantial amount of protein groups and provide sufficient taxonomic identifications if preservation conditions are favorable. However, if preservation conditions are poorer more invasive sampling techniques should be considered.
sampleProcessingProtocol: 100 μL of 0.05 M NH4HCO3 were added to the bone chips and left overnight at 4°C. The supernatant was then transferred to a new tube (AmBic protocol). The bone chips were then demineralised using 150 μL 0.6 M HCl (HCl protocol). Another set of bone chips was left in membrane boxes for a month, whereafter 100 μL 0.05 M NH4HCO3 were heated to 65°C and dragged with a pipette, continuously aspirating and dispensing, over the membrane box’s film surface (membrane box protocol). 100 μL 3.24 M HCl was added to distinct zones and removed for subsequent addition of 100 μL 3.24 M HCl which was then split into two aliquots. One for FASP neutralisation (adding 115 μL 0.05 M NH4HCO3 and filtering with Ultra-4 Centrifugal Filter Unit, Ultracel-3K, Amicon) (acid etch (FASP) protocol) and another for chemical neutralisation (adding 230 μL of 1 M NaOH to reach a pH value of 8) (acid etch (neutralisation) protocol) and dried via vacuum centrifugation. Zones designated for eraser sampling were rubbed with an eraser (Mars® plastic 526 50, Staedler). Eraser residues were collected in tubes and then 100 μL 0.05 M NH4HCO3 were added (eraser protocol). Finally, 30 μm grit size polishing film (PFP Polishing film, 2” Round Aluminium Oxide, PSA, Precision Fiber Products, Inc.) was used for sampling and transferred to tubes of 100 μL 0.05 M NH4HCO3. All samples were then incubated for 1 hour at 65°C and digested at 37°C with 0.8 μg trypsin (Promega) for 18 hours. Peptides were then eluted with Evotips (Evosep, C18 membranes) using Evosep’s (Odense) protocol. Each sample for DIA analysis was separated with reprosil C18 beads (Dr. Maisch) of a diameter of 3 µm and 120 Å pores packed in a 16 cm long silica tube with a 150 µm inner diameter performed on an Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The gradient duration for DIA was 5.6 minutes. One pool sample consisting of 10 μL of each sample was run for DDA analysis with reprosil C18 beads (Dr. Maisch) of a 1.9 µm diameter and 120 Å pores packed in a 16 cm long silica tube with a 150 µm in inner diameter performed on an Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The gradient duration for DDA was 44 minutes. Extraction blanks were processed alongside the samples, and MS data acquisition included injection blanks.
dataProcessingProtocol: The DDA data of the pooled sample was analysed using SpectroMine v3.1 against a subset of 20 Bos taurus and Bos primigenius proteins from the SPIN bone protein database (Rüther et al. 2022) (Project PDX024487). In this search Carbamidomethyl (C) was set as a fixed modification. The variable modifications were acetylation (protein N term), deamidation (NQ) oxidation (PM) Gln -> pyro-Glu, Glu -> pyro-Glu, and Arg -> Orn and up to 6 variable modifications were allowed per peptide. The spectral library generated this way was used to analyse all DIA samples with Spectronaut v18.6 and the same Bos taurus and Bos primigenius database. For Spectronaut all default settings were used.
